title: ASIC loses appeal over Freedom Insurance director ruling
full_text:
ASIC loses appeal over Freedom Insurance director ruling
The Full Federal Court has upheld an earlier ruling that former Freedom Insurance director Keith Cohen did not breach conflicted remuneration laws, dismissing an appeal by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission.
ASIC had claimed Mr Cohen acted unlawfully through his involvement in the Freedom Group’s sales incentive programs that offered Bali holidays and a Vespa motorcycle if targets for a product called Freedom Protection Plan were met.
The corporate watchdog alleged the former director broke conflicted remuneration laws between November 2017 and October 2018 through actions that prioritised sales over customer needs.
ASIC in its appeal said Justice Scott Goodman “erred” in his ruling last year that cleared Mr Cohen but the Full Federal Court disagreed with several points raised by the corporate watchdog.
The Full Federal Court says “none of the relevant findings of fact by the primary judge are challenged” by ASIC in its appeal.
The court also rejected ASIC’s complaint that the primary judge erred in failing to find that Mr Cohen failed to take reasonable steps consistent with director requirements under the Corporations Act.
“The primary judge’s reasons were comprehensive, and his analysis turned on findings of fact which are not challenged in this appeal, including the complexity of the regulatory scheme and changes … No error has been shown."
On ASIC’s claim that the primary judge erred in concluding the former director was entitled to rely on others about potential conflicted remuneration non-compliance, the Full Federal Court said: “Again, this complaint goes nowhere in circumstances where there is no challenge in the appeal to the factual findings … including as to the state of knowledge of Mr Cohen.”
Freedom Insurance was placed in administration in 2020 and deregistered. The company ran into financial trouble after its life insurance sales tactics were exposed in the 2018 Hayne royal commission hearings into financial sector misconduct.
